content: Haemoptysis, or coughing up blood, is a condition that occurs frequently worldwide, with a higher prevalence in low-income countries. It can arise from various causes, many of which are related to infections. Antifibrinolytic agents, which are medications that help prevent the breakdown of blood clots, are often used to manage bleeding in different medical contexts. However, their role in treating haemoptysis remains uncertain. The primary objective of this study was to assess the effectiveness and safety of antifibrinolytic agents in reducing the volume and duration of haemoptysis in both adults and children. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), the Database of Abstracts of Reviews of Effects (DARE), EMBASE, LILACS, and MEDLINE. The search was up to date as of September 19, 2016. Both electronic and manual searches were performed, and reference lists of relevant studies were reviewed to identify additional randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Efforts were also made to locate unpublished RCTs. The inclusion criteria for the review were RCTs that evaluated the effectiveness and safety of antifibrinolytic agents in patients with haemoptysis of any cause or severity. The intervention of interest was the administration of antifibrinolytic agents, compared to either a placebo or no treatment. Data extraction and quality assessment were conducted independently by multiple reviewers. The search identified two RCTs that met the inclusion criteria. The first study, conducted by Tscheikuna in 2002 in Thailand, was a double-blind RCT that evaluated the oral administration of tranexamic acid (TXA), an antifibrinolytic agent, in 46 hospital inpatients and outpatients with haemoptysis of various causes. The second study, conducted by Ruiz in 1994 in Peru, was also a double-blind RCT that assessed the intravenous administration of TXA in 24 hospitalized patients with haemoptysis caused by tuberculosis. When the results of these two studies were pooled, they showed that TXA significantly reduced the duration of bleeding compared to placebo. The weighted mean difference (WMD) in bleeding time was -19.47 hours (95% confidence interval [CI]: -26.90 to -12.03 hours). However, there was considerable variability between the studies (heterogeneity, I² = 52%). Importantly, TXA did not appear to influence the resolution of haemoptysis when assessed seven days after the start of treatment. No adverse effects directly related to the mechanism of action of TXA were reported in either study. Additionally, there was no significant difference in the occurrence of mild side effects between the TXA and placebo groups (odds ratio [OR]: 3.13, 95% CI: 0.80 to 12.24). In conclusion, the evidence available is insufficient to definitively recommend the use of antifibrinolytic agents for the treatment of haemoptysis from any cause. While limited data suggest that these agents may reduce the duration of bleeding, further high-quality research is needed to confirm their effectiveness and safety in this context.
